result.text: Guide to Buenos Aires, Argentina: Microcentro Skip to content Argentina Argentina Argentina by region Maps of Argentina Know everything Argentina hotels Travel Tips When to go Shops Our Tours Our Tours Premium Travel Self-drive tours Themed Tours Cruises in Argentina Getaways to Argentina Private flights Argentina Photos and videos Our agency Our agency Our Team Travel Stories Press Contact Us Back Argentina by region Buenos Aires Province Region Argentina Excepción » Argentina by region » Buenos Aires Province Region » Microcentro Microcentro The Microcentro, the political and economic center of the country The Microcentro, the founding place of the country, is today the seat of business and political institutions. An unofficial neighborhood of Buenos Aires The Microcentro is the business center of the capital, actually straddling two administrative districts: San Nicolás, for the most part, and Montserrat. It boasts a high concentration of offices belonging to national and international companies, banks, and shops. A hive of activity during the week with its millions of employees, the Argentine capital is deserted on weekends. It charms with its blend of old Belle Époque buildings and glass towers. Although spread over only sixty blocks around the Plaza de Mayo, this small district alone houses some of the most important traces of the country's history . Plaza de Mayo Plaza de Mayo, covering approximately 3 hectares, is where the city of Buenos Aires began to take shape and the stage for Argentine independence. Today, a walk around the plaza is a true historical journey . It owes its name to the May Revolution of 1810 , the prelude to Argentine independence proclaimed in 1816. Starting from the plaza, Avenida de Mayo is considered the civic axis, as it connects the Casa Rosada, the seat of executive power, to the Congress of the Nation, the seat of legislative power. Below, behind the Casa Rosada, the Bicentennial Museum offers a glimpse into the history of Argentina. Casa Rosada, Pink House, Argentine Executive Palace On the other side of the square stands the Casa Rosada, the seat of the Argentine Presidency . Its pink color symbolizes the union of the two parties that vied for power in the 19th century: the red of the Federalists and the white of the Unitarians. Due to its symbolic importance, it has witnessed major events that have shaped the country's history, such as the legendary speeches delivered by General Perón and Evita to cheering crowds, and the coup that overthrew General Perón in 1955. Later, it became the site chosen by the Mothers of the May for their marches, which took place every Thursday for 25 years, denouncing the disappearance of their loved ones during the dictatorship. See our special report Cabildo of Buenos Aires On the Plaza de Mayo , opposite the Casa Rosada, stands the white Cabildo building , the seat of government during the colonial era . It was the epicenter of the May Revolution , where the junta of the new government was proclaimed on May 25, 1810. The building dates back to 1748 but has undergone numerous modifications, including the gradual demolition of its wings, which was completed with the construction of Avenida de Mayo in 1889. Today, it houses the National Museum of the Cabildo and the May Revolution. A small craft market is held in its charming courtyard on Thursdays and Fridays. See our photos Buenos Aires Cathedral Right next door is the Metropolitan Cathedral, a neoclassical structure with Corinthian columns. Built in 1812 by Prosper Catelin, a French architect , its façade, in the style of a Greek temple, is inspired by that of the Palais Bourbon in Paris. It houses the mausoleum of General San Martín , a hero of Argentina's independence and liberator, for whom an eternal flame burns in the cathedral square. Apple of Lights The Manzana de las Luces (Block of Lights) is the Jesuit cradle of the neighborhood. Translated as "Block of Lights" in homage to the intellectual and moral enlightenment brought by the Jesuits to the New World, it is the site of the founding of Buenos Aires . Archaeological excavations have unearthed the foundations of the city's earliest buildings, which can be visited. Church of San Ignacio The founding buildings are arranged around one of Buenos Aires' oldest churches: San Ignacio, built by the Jesuits in 1734. Its painted wooden altarpieces and gold-covered scrolls are a superb example of colonial art . Adjacent to it is the Colegio Maximo de San Ignacio, a historic high school where some of the country's most prominent politicians were educated. Underground passages connect the two buildings and were used during the hardships faced by the Society of Jesus following their expulsion from the country at the end of the 18th century. Avila Bookstore Another historical landmark in the area, located just opposite the Church of Saint Ignatius, is the Librairie de Avila, formerly Libreria del Colegio , which impresses with its longevity, dating back to 1785. Also worth mentioning is the La Estrella pharmacy , still operating at the intersection of Defensa and Alsina streets, which impresses with its woodwork adorned with marquetry. Where to shop in the Microcentro? On the other side of the Plaza de Mayo, Florida Street The pedestrian shopping street that begins behind the Cathedral is dotted with superb buildings from the early 20th century, during Buenos Aires' prosperous years. One of the most remarkable is the Güemes Gallery (Florida 150), whose architecture celebrates the richness of Latin America. It's worth taking a closer look at its colossal elevators adorned with copper condors and their grand vaults punctuated with sculpted faces. On the 14th floor, you can enjoy one of the only panoramic views of the city from the center. Fun fact: Antoine de Saint-Exupéry once upon a time lodged in one of the hotel rooms on the top floors of the gallery, during his Argentinian stays dedicated to the Aéropostale line. Where to eat in the Microcentro? Tomo I (Carlos Pellegrini 521) is located on the upper floor of the Hotel Panamericana. It will delight even the most discerning palates thanks to the extraordinary exploration of flavors led by the uncompromising hands of the two sisters who have run it for years. A true gastronomic destination , it is distinguished by its surprise menu, revealed by word of mouth once a week. In a completely different style, the San Ramón Nonato Convent (Reconquista 269) offers, under the arcades of its pretty cloister, a place to nibble on some unpretentious empanadas or milanesas for lunch, away from the surrounding hustle and bustle. Where can I get a coffee in the Microcentro? A little further down Avenue de Mayo, Tortoni café It bears witness to the golden age of Buenos Aires. Founded in 1858, it is among the oldest in the capital. It has stood the test of time with its elegant Belle Époque style, stained-glass windows, and woodwork. An iconic literary café, it still welcomes the Tango Academy of Buenos Aires Once you step through its door, you travel back in time by observing the newspaper clippings and statues of Jorge Luis Borges and Carlos Gardel . See our special report Where to have a drink in the Microcentro? In a friendly atmosphere, El Verde bar welcomes you six nights a week, offering happy hour from 19 pm to 21 pm, followed by live music later in the evening. The menu features a wide variety of alcoholic beverages, including beers and whiskeys. The Sky Bar (Maipú 907) is the city center's most spectacular spot, with its rooftop terrace on the 13th floor of the Pulitzer Hotel. It invites you to enjoy excellent cocktails accompanied by tapas; the tortilla (potato and egg pancake) is a real treat. See our Buenos Aires Rooftop Bar Guide .
